title: Leading by Feelings Versus Principles
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece contrasts two operating systems for leadership: leading by feelings, where mood and emotion drive behavior moment to moment, versus leading by principles, where a fixed set of commitments overrides fluctuating emotional states. The author argues feelings-driven leadership produces inconsistency — investment in people and follow-through on hard tasks rises and falls with mood — while principle-driven leadership sustains difficult but necessary behaviors regardless of how the leader feels that day. Practical advice closes the piece: keep the list of personal principles short enough to memorize and recite them often, treating feelings as visitors rather than authorities.
points: Leaders who operate primarily on mood or emotion tend to be highly inconsistent, since their engagement with people and decisions shifts with whatever recently influenced their state.
Principles function as a countermeasure to fluctuating feelings, pushing leaders to do necessary things (hard conversations, preparation, hard workouts) regardless of momentary mood.
The ideal is a tight, memorable set of core principles — too many becomes robotic, too few lets feelings dominate decision-making.
Leaders are advised to write down and regularly recite their non-negotiable commitments so they hold under emotional pressure.
quotes: Their behaviors and choices reflect what they are feeling at any given moment. How they feel determines what they do or don’t do.
Almost by definition, people who lead and live by feelings are highly inconsistent.
As their feelings change, so do their behaviors and decisions. Leading and living by feelings is a rollercoaster.
The core set of principles good leaders live and lead by allows them to stick to their guns. Principles get them to the gym when they don’t have the energy.
Consider writing down the principles you want to lead and live by. Keep the list of personal rules and commitments tight enough so you can memorize them.
